scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document is an EHR-based retrospective cohort study (RECOVER Initiative, Clinical Infectious Diseases 2025) estimating Long COVID incidence proportions in adults and children across three nationwide EHR networks (N3C, PCORnet, PEDSnet); Lyme disease is never mentioned.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed epidemiological study, not a cost study, that used electronic health record (EHR) data from three large U.S. research networks to estimate how often people who had COVID-19 went on to develop Long COVID, using several different computable 'definitions' (algorithms) of the condition. Overall, 10.2%-25.9% of adults and 4.0% of children who tested positive for COVID-19 were identified as having Long COVID within 180 days, depending on which network's algorithm was used; after subtracting a background rate seen in COVID-negative comparison groups, the 'excess' incidence attributable to COVID-19 was estimated at about 5%-6% in adults and 1.4% in children. The study found Long COVID risk was consistently higher in older adults, women, and people with more severe acute COVID-19 or more pre-existing health conditions. The document does not report any direct medical costs, non-medical costs, productivity loss, or caregiving burden - its contribution is solely to the question of how many people are affected and who is at higher risk, not what it costs them.

contextual_issues: Quality-of-life impact, functional limitations, psychological distress, and higher numbers of healthcare visits are mentioned in the Introduction as consequences of Long COVID, but these are attributed to a separate cited study (ref. 4), not quantified within this study's own EHR data.

Variation in healthcare access by gender, race/ethnicity, rurality, and other structural/social determinants of health is noted as a limitation affecting who gets diagnosed and documented, but no access-barrier metric is quantified.

The requirement that 'patients must seek care as a prerequisite for having documentation available' is raised as a limitation (implying diagnostic/detection delay), but no specific delay interval or care-seeking-barrier figure is reported.
Repeated care-seeking, insurance barriers, direct medical/non-medical costs, lost income, and caregiving time are not mentioned anywhere in this document.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, direct non-medical cost, or indirect/productivity-loss data of any kind are reported; monetizing these incidence and risk-factor findings would require an entirely separate cost dataset not present in this document.

No patient-reported outcome or chart-review validation is available to confirm the EHR-coded computable phenotypes against actual patient experience; the authors themselves identify this as needed future work.
No follow-up beyond 180 days (or 270 days in the harmonized analysis) is reported, so no long-term or lifetime burden trajectory can be derived from this study.
Patient-level SARS-CoV-2 variant and complete vaccination data were unavailable, which the authors state limits interpretation of temporal and variant-driven incidence patterns.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the N3C adult incidence estimate (10.2%, 3,800,805 patients, machine-learning-based phenotype) with the PCORnet adult estimate (25.9%, 1,870,810 patients, rules-based ICD-10-category phenotype) into one national average - they use structurally different computable phenotypes applied to different (only partially overlapping) EHR populations, even though both use the same 180-day measurement window.

Do not pool 'crude' incidence proportions with 'excess' (control-subtracted) incidence proportions - these are different measurement constructs: crude incidence is the raw proportion of COVID-positive patients meeting the phenotype, while excess incidence subtracts a COVID-negative control group's background rate and is explicitly described by the authors as a lower-bound estimate.

The harmonized (NASEM-aligned) incidence proportions (N3C 12.6%, PCORnet 9.6%) use a 270-day measurement window, differing from the 180-day window used in each network's own primary phenotype - these should not be placed in a single low-to-high range with the 180-day estimates without noting the different time windows.

Pediatric (PEDSnet, ≤21 years, 727,994 patients, requires 2 diagnoses ≥28 days apart in a symptom cluster) and adult (N3C/PCORnet, >22 years) incidence estimates are structurally different populations and definitions and must not be combined into a single 'all ages' burden figure.

Historical (first 5 months of 2019) and contemporary (first 5 months of 2021) COVID-negative control groups used to estimate excess incidence are different time periods/populations with different healthcare-utilization patterns (the authors note historical controls may have higher utilization while contemporary controls may include false-negative/undocumented infections); excess-incidence figures derived from each should not be treated as interchangeable.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The study found female patients had a significantly higher adjusted risk of developing long COVID than male patients across all three networks: N3C adjusted hazard ratio 1.41 (95% CI 1.41-1.42, P<.001), PCORnet adjusted hazard ratio 1.14 (95% CI 1.12-1.14, P<.001), and PEDSnet (pediatric) adjusted hazard ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.14-1.22, P<.001).

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The study identifies long COVID via EHR diagnosis codes (ICD-10 U09.9, B94.8, M35.81) and computable phenotypes built on ICD-10-coded diagnoses across three EHR networks (N3C, PCORnet, PEDSnet); the authors themselves state in the Limitations section that 'the nature of EHR data may lead to underreporting or missed diagnoses of COVID-19 and long COVID, especially as patients must seek care as a prerequisite for having documentation available,' and note underrepresentation of non-academic medical centers and variation in healthcare access by gender, race/ethnicity, and rurality.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a lack of a gold-standard, unified case definition for Long COVID: each EHR network uses its own distinct computable phenotype, published literature estimates range from 6% to over 50%, and even the newly published NASEM definition is described by the authors as 'challenging to apply to research,' requiring further work to adapt it to EHR-based studies.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Introduction states 'Given the pluralistic nature of the illness and lack of a gold standard, various case definitions for long COVID have been operationalized by researchers,' and the Discussion states NASEM's guidelines 'are challenging to apply to research... further work is needed to improve their application to EHR-based research.'

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document would be useful to public health surveillance planners, researchers, and clinical care teams interested in the scale and demographic/clinical risk pattern of Long COVID, not to parties needing cost figures, since none are reported here. Patients/advocates could use the risk-factor findings (older age, female sex, severity of acute illness, pre-existing conditions) to understand who is more likely to be affected. Payers/policy audiences could use the range of incidence estimates to gauge potential population scale, but would need to source cost data elsewhere since this document contains none, and should not treat the different networks' and definitions' estimates as a single confidence interval.
use_cases: Public health and health-system planners could use the range of crude vs. excess incidence proportions (by network and by definition) as alternate scenario inputs for estimating the population scale of Long COVID needing follow-up care capacity, while keeping clear that each network's point estimate reflects a different computable phenotype, population, and (for the harmonized analysis) a different follow-up window.

Clinicians and care-delivery teams could use the reported risk factors (age 65+, female sex, acute COVID-19 severity including ICU-level hospitalization, and pre-existing comorbidity burden) to identify which patient subgroups most warrant closer post-COVID-19 follow-up for possible Long COVID.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document is an EHR-based retrospective cohort study (RECOVER Initiative, Clinical Infectious Diseases 2025) estimating Long COVID incidence proportions in adults and children across three nationwide EHR networks (N3C, PCORnet, PEDSnet); Lyme disease is never mentioned.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed epidemiological study, not a cost study, that used electronic health record (EHR) data from three large U.S. research networks to estimate how often people who had COVID-19 went on to develop Long COVID, using several different computable 'definitions' (algorithms) of the condition. Overall, 10.2%-25.9% of adults and 4.0% of children who tested positive for COVID-19 were identified as having Long COVID within 180 days, depending on which network's algorithm was used; after subtracting a background rate seen in COVID-negative comparison groups, the 'excess' incidence attributable to COVID-19 was estimated at about 5%-6% in adults and 1.4% in children. The study found Long COVID risk was consistently higher in older adults, women, and people with more severe acute COVID-19 or more pre-existing health conditions. The document does not report any direct medical costs, non-medical costs, productivity loss, or caregiving burden - its contribution is solely to the question of how many people are affected and who is at higher risk, not what it costs them.

contextual_issues: Quality-of-life impact, functional limitations, psychological distress, and higher numbers of healthcare visits are mentioned in the Introduction as consequences of Long COVID, but these are attributed to a separate cited study (ref. 4), not quantified within this study's own EHR data.

Variation in healthcare access by gender, race/ethnicity, rurality, and other structural/social determinants of health is noted as a limitation affecting who gets diagnosed and documented, but no access-barrier metric is quantified.

The requirement that 'patients must seek care as a prerequisite for having documentation available' is raised as a limitation (implying diagnostic/detection delay), but no specific delay interval or care-seeking-barrier figure is reported.
Repeated care-seeking, insurance barriers, direct medical/non-medical costs, lost income, and caregiving time are not mentioned anywhere in this document.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, direct non-medical cost, or indirect/productivity-loss data of any kind are reported; monetizing these incidence and risk-factor findings would require an entirely separate cost dataset not present in this document.

No patient-reported outcome or chart-review validation is available to confirm the EHR-coded computable phenotypes against actual patient experience; the authors themselves identify this as needed future work.
No follow-up beyond 180 days (or 270 days in the harmonized analysis) is reported, so no long-term or lifetime burden trajectory can be derived from this study.
Patient-level SARS-CoV-2 variant and complete vaccination data were unavailable, which the authors state limits interpretation of temporal and variant-driven incidence patterns.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the N3C adult incidence estimate (10.2%, 3,800,805 patients, machine-learning-based phenotype) with the PCORnet adult estimate (25.9%, 1,870,810 patients, rules-based ICD-10-category phenotype) into one national average - they use structurally different computable phenotypes applied to different (only partially overlapping) EHR populations, even though both use the same 180-day measurement window.

Do not pool 'crude' incidence proportions with 'excess' (control-subtracted) incidence proportions - these are different measurement constructs: crude incidence is the raw proportion of COVID-positive patients meeting the phenotype, while excess incidence subtracts a COVID-negative control group's background rate and is explicitly described by the authors as a lower-bound estimate.

The harmonized (NASEM-aligned) incidence proportions (N3C 12.6%, PCORnet 9.6%) use a 270-day measurement window, differing from the 180-day window used in each network's own primary phenotype - these should not be placed in a single low-to-high range with the 180-day estimates without noting the different time windows.

Pediatric (PEDSnet, ≤21 years, 727,994 patients, requires 2 diagnoses ≥28 days apart in a symptom cluster) and adult (N3C/PCORnet, >22 years) incidence estimates are structurally different populations and definitions and must not be combined into a single 'all ages' burden figure.

Historical (first 5 months of 2019) and contemporary (first 5 months of 2021) COVID-negative control groups used to estimate excess incidence are different time periods/populations with different healthcare-utilization patterns (the authors note historical controls may have higher utilization while contemporary controls may include false-negative/undocumented infections); excess-incidence figures derived from each should not be treated as interchangeable.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The study found female patients had a significantly higher adjusted risk of developing long COVID than male patients across all three networks: N3C adjusted hazard ratio 1.41 (95% CI 1.41-1.42, P<.001), PCORnet adjusted hazard ratio 1.14 (95% CI 1.12-1.14, P<.001), and PEDSnet (pediatric) adjusted hazard ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.14-1.22, P<.001).

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The study identifies long COVID via EHR diagnosis codes (ICD-10 U09.9, B94.8, M35.81) and computable phenotypes built on ICD-10-coded diagnoses across three EHR networks (N3C, PCORnet, PEDSnet); the authors themselves state in the Limitations section that 'the nature of EHR data may lead to underreporting or missed diagnoses of COVID-19 and long COVID, especially as patients must seek care as a prerequisite for having documentation available,' and note underrepresentation of non-academic medical centers and variation in healthcare access by gender, race/ethnicity, and rurality.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a lack of a gold-standard, unified case definition for Long COVID: each EHR network uses its own distinct computable phenotype, published literature estimates range from 6% to over 50%, and even the newly published NASEM definition is described by the authors as 'challenging to apply to research,' requiring further work to adapt it to EHR-based studies.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Introduction states 'Given the pluralistic nature of the illness and lack of a gold standard, various case definitions for long COVID have been operationalized by researchers,' and the Discussion states NASEM's guidelines 'are challenging to apply to research... further work is needed to improve their application to EHR-based research.'

spec.title: Long COVID Incidence and Risk-Factor Explorer (RECOVER EHR Networks Study)
spec.boundary: This simulator represents only incidence proportions, background-adjusted ('excess') incidence estimates, and sex-based risk-factor hazard ratios for Long COVID reported from three U.S. electronic health record (EHR) research networks (N3C, PCORnet, PEDSnet), measured within 180 days (or 270 days for a harmonized definition) of a documented COVID-19 infection, 2020-2023. It omits all direct medical costs, non-medical costs, lost income, caregiving time, long-term (beyond 180-270 day) trajectories, and patient-reported validation, none of which this document reports.

takeaway.patient: This study looked at electronic health records from three large research networks and found that, among people who tested positive for COVID-19, somewhere between about 10% and 26% of adults (and about 4% of children) were later coded with Long COVID within six months, depending on which network and definition was used. After comparing against people who did not have COVID-19, the researchers estimated a smaller 'excess' share attributable to COVID-19 itself - about 5-6 percentage points in adults and about 1.4 percentage points in children - which the study describes as a lower-bound (likely-undercounted) estimate, not a complete count. The study also found that women had a higher statistically-adjusted likelihood of developing Long COVID than men in all three networks (roughly 1.14 to 1.41 times the risk), and that risk was higher at older ages and with more severe acute illness.
takeaway.care: Across three EHR networks, reported Long COVID incidence proportions among COVID-19-positive patients ranged widely (about 10% to 26% in adults within 180 days; about 4% in children), reflecting different computable phenotypes (a rules-based ICD-10 approach versus a machine-learning approach) applied to different, only partially overlapping populations - not a single agreed-upon case definition. Risk was consistently higher with older age, female sex, more severe acute illness (including ICU-level hospitalization in children, the strongest single factor identified), and pre-existing conditions. The authors note that care-seeking is a prerequisite for a case to appear in EHR data at all, meaning documented incidence likely understates true occurrence.
takeaway.policy: Three EHR networks produced adult Long COVID incidence estimates ranging from about 10% to 26% of COVID-19-positive adults within 180 days, and about 4% in children, using structurally different computable phenotypes and populations that the authors say should not be pooled into one national figure. After subtracting background rates seen in COVID-negative comparison groups, excess incidence attributable to COVID-19 was estimated at about 5-6 percentage points in adults and about 1.4 percentage points in children - described by the authors as a lower-bound estimate given EHR-based underreporting. Female sex was associated with significantly higher adjusted risk in all three networks (hazard ratios about 1.14 to 1.41). No cost data of any kind are reported in this document.

patient: Note that this study found higher reported likelihood of Long COVID among older adults, women, and people who had more severe acute COVID-19 illness (including intensive-care-level treatment in children) - this may be worth raising in a conversation with a clinician about follow-up care.

Because the study notes that only documented, care-seeking visits could be counted, consider discussing with a clinician what ongoing symptoms after COVID-19, even mild or intermittent ones, might be worth a follow-up visit.

Treat the different percentage ranges in this study as a general sense of scale from different research networks and definitions, not as a precise personal probability, since the study itself says these estimates should not be combined into one number.
care: Consider using the study's reported risk factors (older age, female sex, more severe or ICU-level acute COVID-19, pre-existing conditions) as a starting point for flagging patients who may warrant proactive post-COVID-19 follow-up scheduling.

This study's finding that incidence estimates vary widely (roughly 10% to 26% in adults) depending on which computable phenotype was applied may be worth checking against your own site's Long COVID case-identification or referral criteria.

Because the authors note care-seeking is a prerequisite for a case to be documented, symptom screening at routine visits for patients with a COVID-19 history could be worth discussing as a way to surface under-documented cases.

The study notes no single case definition is agreed upon (even the newer NASEM definition is described as hard to apply to EHR research) - this gap may be worth considering when reviewing how your own program documents or codes Long COVID.
policy: Use the reported range of crude incidence estimates (about 10% to 26% of COVID-19-positive adults, and about 4% of children, depending on network and definition) as alternate planning scenarios for post-COVID-19 care capacity rather than averaging them into a single national rate.

Treat the excess incidence estimates (about 5-6 percentage points in adults, about 1.4 percentage points in children) as lower-bound figures per the study's own framing, since they rely on EHR diagnosis coding that may miss undocumented cases; source cost data separately, as none is reported here.

Consider the study's note that no standardized Long COVID case definition exists across EHR networks (and that the NASEM definition remains difficult to apply to EHR-based research) as a research-standardization gap that may warrant investment.

Track that female sex was associated with significantly higher adjusted risk of Long COVID across all three networks (adjusted hazard ratios about 1.14 to 1.41), which may be relevant for demographic-targeted research or outreach prioritization.

inputs.label: N3C adult crude incidence (% of COVID-positive adults)
inputs.source: Abstract and Results, p.1252 (N3C network, machine-learning-based computable phenotype, index infections within 180 days); 0-50 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is N3C's reported share of COVID-positive adults identified with Long COVID using its own machine-learning-based phenotype; moving it shows how sensitive population-scale planning is to which network's algorithm is used.

inputs.label: PCORnet adult crude incidence (% of COVID-positive adults)
inputs.source: Abstract and Results, p.1252 (PCORnet network, rules-based ICD-10-category computable phenotype, index infections within 180 days); 0-50 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PCORnet's reported share of COVID-positive adults identified with Long COVID using its own rules-based phenotype; comparing it against N3C's figure below illustrates how much estimates differ by computable-phenotype design, not by accuracy.

inputs.label: PEDSnet child crude incidence (% of COVID-positive children)
inputs.source: Abstract and Results, p.1252 (PEDSnet network, pediatric phenotype requiring 2 diagnoses 28+ days apart, index infections within 180 days); 0-20 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PEDSnet's reported share of COVID-positive children identified with Long COVID; it is structurally a different population and definition from the adult figures and should not be averaged with them.

inputs.label: N3C adult excess incidence (percentage points)
inputs.source: Control Group Analysis, Results, p.1257 (N3C, contemporary 2021 COVID-negative control baseline); 0-15 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is N3C's crude incidence minus its COVID-negative control group's background rate, described by the study as a lower-bound estimate of incidence attributable to COVID-19; moving it shows how much of the crude figure above reflects background diagnosis rates versus COVID-19 itself.

inputs.label: PCORnet adult excess incidence (percentage points)
inputs.source: Control Group Analysis, Results, p.1257 (PCORnet, contemporary 2021 COVID-negative control baseline); 0-15 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PCORnet's background-rate-subtracted excess incidence estimate; comparing it with N3C's figure shows the two networks arrived at similar excess ranges despite very different crude incidence figures.

inputs.label: PEDSnet child excess incidence (percentage points)
inputs.source: Control Group Analysis, Results, p.1257 (PEDSnet, contemporary 2021 COVID-negative control baseline); 0-10 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PEDSnet's background-rate-subtracted excess incidence estimate for children, substantially smaller than the adult figures, illustrating the study's finding that excess risk attributable to COVID-19 was lower in children.

inputs.label: N3C adjusted hazard ratio, female vs male
inputs.source: Multivariable Analysis, Results, p.1253 and Table 3 (N3C network); 1.0-2.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is N3C's statistically adjusted risk of Long COVID in women relative to men; a value above 1.0 means higher risk in women, and this input lets a reader compare the size of that sex difference against the other two networks below.

inputs.label: PCORnet adjusted hazard ratio, female vs male
inputs.source: Multivariable Analysis, Results, p.1253 and Table 3 (PCORnet network); 1.0-2.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PCORnet's statistically adjusted risk of Long COVID in women relative to men; comparing it with N3C's figure shows both networks found higher female risk, but of different sizes.

outputs.label: PCORnet minus N3C adult crude incidence (positive = PCORnet estimate higher; negative = N3C estimate higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the two networks' crude incidence estimates for adults. The study attributes this gap to differing computable phenotypes (rules-based versus machine-learning) applied to different, only partially overlapping populations, not to one network being more accurate than the other; the study instructs readers not to pool these into a single figure.

outputs.label: N3C adult excess incidence attributable to COVID-19
outputs.interpretation: This is N3C's crude adult incidence minus its contemporary COVID-negative control group's background rate. The study describes this as a lower-bound estimate because EHR-coded diagnoses likely miss some true cases; a higher value means a larger measured share of Long COVID is attributable to COVID-19 beyond background diagnosis rates.

outputs.label: PCORnet adult excess incidence attributable to COVID-19
outputs.interpretation: This is PCORnet's crude adult incidence minus its contemporary COVID-negative control group's background rate, also described by the study as a lower-bound estimate; comparing it to N3C's excess figure shows the two networks converge more closely here than on crude incidence alone.

outputs.label: PEDSnet child excess incidence attributable to COVID-19
outputs.interpretation: This is PEDSnet's crude child incidence minus its contemporary COVID-negative control group's background rate, described by the study as a lower-bound estimate; its smaller size relative to the adult excess-incidence figures reflects the study's finding of lower excess risk in children.

outputs.label: N3C minus PCORnet adjusted hazard ratio for female sex (positive = N3C found a larger female-vs-male risk difference; negative = PCORnet found a larger difference)
outputs.interpretation: Both networks found a statistically significantly higher adjusted risk of Long COVID in women than men (N3C hazard ratio 1.41; PCORnet hazard ratio 1.14), but the size of that difference varied by network and population. This gap shows how much the two networks' estimates of the female-sex risk difference diverge; it should not be read as evidence one network's estimate is more correct.

scenarios.label: Harmonized 270-day definition
scenarios.goal: Shows how the network gap changes using the NASEM-aligned 270-day definition.
scenarios.description: Substituting each network's own reported harmonized incidence (N3C 12.6%, PCORnet 9.6%, measured within a 270-day window) for their 180-day crude phenotypes shows how the adult incidence gap changes under the study's alternate, supplementary NASEM-aligned definition.

scenarios.label: Pediatric female-risk value in N3C
scenarios.goal: Tests whether N3C's larger female-risk gap holds using the pediatric estimate instead.
scenarios.description: Replacing N3C's adult female-vs-male hazard ratio (1.41) with PEDSnet's pediatric value (1.17) shows how the female-hazard-ratio gap would look if N3C's adult risk differential matched the smaller pediatric one the study reports in the same table.

scenarios.label: PCORnet matches N3C's female-risk estimate
scenarios.goal: Tests how sensitive the cross-network gap is to each network's own phenotype.
scenarios.description: Setting PCORnet's female-vs-male hazard ratio to N3C's own reported adult value (1.41) instead of PCORnet's lower value (1.14) shows how much of the reported female-hazard-ratio gap traces to differences between the two networks' computable phenotypes.

package.documentation:
## About this simulator

This tool is built from a peer-reviewed RECOVER Initiative study (Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2025) using electronic health record (EHR) data from three U.S. research networks - N3C, PCORnet (both adults), and PEDSnet (children) - to estimate how often people documented with COVID-19 were later identified with Long COVID using each network's own computable phenotype (a rules-based or machine-learning algorithm applied to diagnosis codes), within 180 days of infection (index events March 2020-July 2023).

**What the inputs represent:** Crude incidence proportions are the raw share of COVID-19-positive patients meeting each network's phenotype. Excess incidence proportions subtract the rate seen in a contemporary (2021) COVID-negative control group, which the authors describe as a lower-bound estimate of incidence attributable to COVID-19 itself - not a confirmed true count. Hazard ratios describe statistically adjusted risk differences by sex. All slider ranges beyond the documented default values are assumed exploration bounds chosen for this simulator, not reported uncertainty intervals from the study.

**Sex differences:** The study found women had significantly higher adjusted risk of Long COVID than men in all three networks (hazard ratios 1.41 in N3C, 1.14 in PCORnet, 1.17 in PEDSnet), which this simulator keeps as separate, comparable inputs rather than collapsing into one pooled figure.

**Limitations carried from the source:** Because Long COVID is identified through EHR diagnosis codes (ICD-10 U09.9, B94.8, M35.81), the authors note that patients must seek and receive documented care to be counted at all, and that healthcare access varies by gender, race/ethnicity, and rurality - meaning both the crude and excess incidence figures likely undercount the true population burden, not just reflect it completely. Separately, the authors describe a lack of any gold-standard case definition for Long COVID: each network uses its own phenotype, published estimates elsewhere range from about 6% to over 50%, and even the newer NASEM consensus definition is described as difficult to apply to EHR-based research - a systemic evidence-infrastructure gap distinct from the accuracy of any single estimate here.

**What this simulator does not cover:** No direct medical costs, non-medical costs, income loss, or caregiving burden are reported anywhere in this study; any cost-based decision requires separate data sources. No follow-up beyond 180-270 days is available, so no long-term burden trajectory can be derived. The different networks' and definitions' estimates should not be pooled into one national figure, per the study's own guidance.

care: Consider using the study's reported risk factors (older age, female sex, more severe or ICU-level acute COVID-19, pre-existing conditions) as a starting point for flagging patients who may warrant proactive post-COVID-19 follow-up scheduling.

This study's finding that incidence estimates vary widely (roughly 10% to 26% in adults) depending on which computable phenotype was applied may be worth checking against your own site's Long COVID case-identification or referral criteria.

Because the authors note care-seeking is a prerequisite for a case to be documented, symptom screening at routine visits for patients with a COVID-19 history could be worth discussing as a way to surface under-documented cases.

The study notes no single case definition is agreed upon (even the newer NASEM definition is described as hard to apply to EHR research) - this gap may be worth considering when reviewing how your own program documents or codes Long COVID.
policy: Use the reported range of crude incidence estimates (about 10% to 26% of COVID-19-positive adults, and about 4% of children, depending on network and definition) as alternate planning scenarios for post-COVID-19 care capacity rather than averaging them into a single national rate.

Treat the excess incidence estimates (about 5-6 percentage points in adults, about 1.4 percentage points in children) as lower-bound figures per the study's own framing, since they rely on EHR diagnosis coding that may miss undocumented cases; source cost data separately, as none is reported here.

Consider the study's note that no standardized Long COVID case definition exists across EHR networks (and that the NASEM definition remains difficult to apply to EHR-based research) as a research-standardization gap that may warrant investment.

Track that female sex was associated with significantly higher adjusted risk of Long COVID across all three networks (adjusted hazard ratios about 1.14 to 1.41), which may be relevant for demographic-targeted research or outreach prioritization.

inputs.label: N3C adult crude incidence (% of COVID-positive adults)
inputs.source: Abstract and Results, p.1252 (N3C network, machine-learning-based computable phenotype, index infections within 180 days); 0-50 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is N3C's reported share of COVID-positive adults identified with Long COVID using its own machine-learning-based phenotype; moving it shows how sensitive population-scale planning is to which network's algorithm is used.

inputs.label: PCORnet adult crude incidence (% of COVID-positive adults)
inputs.source: Abstract and Results, p.1252 (PCORnet network, rules-based ICD-10-category computable phenotype, index infections within 180 days); 0-50 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PCORnet's reported share of COVID-positive adults identified with Long COVID using its own rules-based phenotype; comparing it against N3C's figure below illustrates how much estimates differ by computable-phenotype design, not by accuracy.

inputs.label: PEDSnet child crude incidence (% of COVID-positive children)
inputs.source: Abstract and Results, p.1252 (PEDSnet network, pediatric phenotype requiring 2 diagnoses 28+ days apart, index infections within 180 days); 0-20 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PEDSnet's reported share of COVID-positive children identified with Long COVID; it is structurally a different population and definition from the adult figures and should not be averaged with them.

inputs.label: N3C adult excess incidence (percentage points)
inputs.source: Control Group Analysis, Results, p.1257 (N3C, contemporary 2021 COVID-negative control baseline); 0-15 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is N3C's crude incidence minus its COVID-negative control group's background rate, described by the study as a lower-bound estimate of incidence attributable to COVID-19; moving it shows how much of the crude figure above reflects background diagnosis rates versus COVID-19 itself.

inputs.label: PCORnet adult excess incidence (percentage points)
inputs.source: Control Group Analysis, Results, p.1257 (PCORnet, contemporary 2021 COVID-negative control baseline); 0-15 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PCORnet's background-rate-subtracted excess incidence estimate; comparing it with N3C's figure shows the two networks arrived at similar excess ranges despite very different crude incidence figures.

inputs.label: PEDSnet child excess incidence (percentage points)
inputs.source: Control Group Analysis, Results, p.1257 (PEDSnet, contemporary 2021 COVID-negative control baseline); 0-10 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PEDSnet's background-rate-subtracted excess incidence estimate for children, substantially smaller than the adult figures, illustrating the study's finding that excess risk attributable to COVID-19 was lower in children.

inputs.label: N3C adjusted hazard ratio, female vs male
inputs.source: Multivariable Analysis, Results, p.1253 and Table 3 (N3C network); 1.0-2.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is N3C's statistically adjusted risk of Long COVID in women relative to men; a value above 1.0 means higher risk in women, and this input lets a reader compare the size of that sex difference against the other two networks below.

inputs.label: PCORnet adjusted hazard ratio, female vs male
inputs.source: Multivariable Analysis, Results, p.1253 and Table 3 (PCORnet network); 1.0-2.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is PCORnet's statistically adjusted risk of Long COVID in women relative to men; comparing it with N3C's figure shows both networks found higher female risk, but of different sizes.

outputs.label: PCORnet minus N3C adult crude incidence (positive = PCORnet estimate higher; negative = N3C estimate higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the two networks' crude incidence estimates for adults. The study attributes this gap to differing computable phenotypes (rules-based versus machine-learning) applied to different, only partially overlapping populations, not to one network being more accurate than the other; the study instructs readers not to pool these into a single figure.

outputs.label: N3C adult excess incidence attributable to COVID-19
outputs.interpretation: This is N3C's crude adult incidence minus its contemporary COVID-negative control group's background rate. The study describes this as a lower-bound estimate because EHR-coded diagnoses likely miss some true cases; a higher value means a larger measured share of Long COVID is attributable to COVID-19 beyond background diagnosis rates.

outputs.label: PCORnet adult excess incidence attributable to COVID-19
outputs.interpretation: This is PCORnet's crude adult incidence minus its contemporary COVID-negative control group's background rate, also described by the study as a lower-bound estimate; comparing it to N3C's excess figure shows the two networks converge more closely here than on crude incidence alone.

outputs.label: PEDSnet child excess incidence attributable to COVID-19
outputs.interpretation: This is PEDSnet's crude child incidence minus its contemporary COVID-negative control group's background rate, described by the study as a lower-bound estimate; its smaller size relative to the adult excess-incidence figures reflects the study's finding of lower excess risk in children.

outputs.label: N3C minus PCORnet adjusted hazard ratio for female sex (positive = N3C found a larger female-vs-male risk difference; negative = PCORnet found a larger difference)
outputs.interpretation: Both networks found a statistically significantly higher adjusted risk of Long COVID in women than men (N3C hazard ratio 1.41; PCORnet hazard ratio 1.14), but the size of that difference varied by network and population. This gap shows how much the two networks' estimates of the female-sex risk difference diverge; it should not be read as evidence one network's estimate is more correct.

scenarios.label: Harmonized 270-day definition
scenarios.goal: Shows how the network gap changes using the NASEM-aligned 270-day definition.
scenarios.description: Substituting each network's own reported harmonized incidence (N3C 12.6%, PCORnet 9.6%, measured within a 270-day window) for their 180-day crude phenotypes shows how the adult incidence gap changes under the study's alternate, supplementary NASEM-aligned definition.

scenarios.label: Pediatric female-risk value in N3C
scenarios.goal: Tests whether N3C's larger female-risk gap holds using the pediatric estimate instead.
scenarios.description: Replacing N3C's adult female-vs-male hazard ratio (1.41) with PEDSnet's pediatric value (1.17) shows how the female-hazard-ratio gap would look if N3C's adult risk differential matched the smaller pediatric one the study reports in the same table.

scenarios.label: PCORnet matches N3C's female-risk estimate
scenarios.goal: Tests how sensitive the cross-network gap is to each network's own phenotype.
scenarios.description: Setting PCORnet's female-vs-male hazard ratio to N3C's own reported adult value (1.41) instead of PCORnet's lower value (1.14) shows how much of the reported female-hazard-ratio gap traces to differences between the two networks' computable phenotypes.
